Adaptive multi-objective optimization for emergency evacuation at
metro stations
Kai Guo 1, Limao Zhang 2,*
1 Ph.D. Candidate, School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, Singapore 639798
2 Assistant Professor, School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, Singapore 639798.
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Emergency evacuation
Metro stations
Pedestrian behaviors
Evacuation prediction
Adaptive multi-objective optimization
A B S T R A C T
Evacuation is a critical issue at metro stations, where damage, or even death, could be caused due to unexpected
accidents if without proper evacuation. Multi-objectives are often desired in the evacuation management, and
evacuation strategies should be tailored due to the dynamic features of overcrowded passengers and high un­
certainty at the metro stations. A simulation-based approach integrating Light Gradient Boosting Machine
(LightGBM) and Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III) is proposed to realize the automatic
evacuation evaluation and adaptive optimization at metro stations. A framework consisting of 3 objectives and 9
influential factors is developed for the evacuation evaluation and adaptive optimization. A LightGBM based
meta-model is used to construct the relationship between influential factors and objectives. A LightGBM and
NSGA-III integrated optimization algorithm is employed to automatically evaluate the evacuation events and
seek the adaptive strategies for the station renovation in order to achieve a safe evacuation under specific
conditions. A station model simulating a metro station in Singapore is constructed to test the effectiveness and
applicability of the proposed approach. It is found that (1) Among 50 target station based cases, 33 failing cases
(at least one of the objectives fails) are identified, and the automatic evaluation results indicate the studied metro
station could successfully evacuate the passengers when the passenger volume is no more than 1000, but it is
very likely to fail when a higher volume exists; (2) Adaptive optimization strategies can be found for every
different scenario, and an average 24.8% of the improvement degree can be achieved for all scenarios; (3) The
adaptive multi-objective optimization is more cost-effective, presenting an average cost efficiency 2.04, which is
significantly higher than the average of the non-adaptive optimization cost efficiency, 0.57. The novelty of this
research lies in that (a) A LightGBM-based meta-model is built to construct the relationship between desired
multi-objectives and the influential factors, which lays the foundation for the evacuation management from
multi-objective optimization perspective; (b) The LightGBM and NSGA-III integrated model can realize the
automatic evacuation evaluation and accordingly provide the adaptive strategies under specific conditions.
1. Introduction
Evacuation is an indispensable protection measure to reduce emer­
gency risks and mitigate the consequences of accidents. Even though
countless efforts have been put to guarantee the safety, accidents at
metro stations could still happen. For example, due to the unexpected
heavy rain, the Haitansi and Shakou road metro stations were flooded in
Zhengzhou, China. More than 500 passengers were timely evacuated,
but still the casualty was confirmed as 14 in the end [1]. An emergency
shutdown happened at the Joo Koon metro station of Singapore on 15
November 2017 since two trains crashed, leading to 36 passengers and 2
staff being injured [2]. Due to the lack of effective emergency response
measures and evacuation strategies, the Daegu metro station fire acci­
dent in South Korea killed 192 and injured 151 [3]. To guarantee the
safety and minimize the potential damage, appropriate and timely
evacuation strategies become critical. More importantly, evacuation
strategies should be tailored according to the specific features of the
target metro stations, where the particular conditions may require
different strategies to effectively manage the evacuation events. That is,
not just the generally applicable but the tailored strategies, i.e., adaptive
strategies to specific conditions, are critical for the safety management
of metro stations in response to the emergencies.

The complexity nature of evacuation brings difficulties and chal­
lenges for the evacuation management and renovation, especially at
metro station scenarios, where densely crowded passengers, relatively
narrowed space and high uncertainty are the norm [38,39]. First, many
influential factors are involved, and different criteria are investigated to
evaluate the evacuation at metro stations. For example, the competi­
tiveness of evacuees was studied as the main factor causing dangerous
clogs [4]. The proper guide was considered as the most important factor
that could guide evacuees to avoid collision and find the exits effectively
[5]. In the study of Han et al. [6], the utilization rate of exits, obstacles,
and crowd decentralizing rate were believed as the critical factors
decisive for an effective evacuation. The number and positions of leaders
could exert a remarkable effect on the evacuation, especially under the
limited visibility scenarios. Second, a complex and even conflicting
relationship exists between the objectives deciding the success of the
evacuation. Taking the evacuation time and density as an example, too
much emphasis on reducing the evacuation time may cause a potential
high-density risk, and too much emphasis on reducing the density could
lead to a longer evacuation time, which may require more evacuation
resources. The influence of the presence of obstacles during the evacu­
ation site could also be elusive. As the obstacle was found beneficial for
improving the flow rate in some studies but unfavorable due to the
congestion and danger caused by it in other cases [7]. To sum up,
different objectives are often desired, and they have to be considered
simultaneously for the safe evacuation at metro stations, i.e., it is
necessary to consider the evacuation management from the
multi-objective optimization (MOO) perspective. Besides, it could be
quite challenging to accurately build the relationship between the
desired objectives and the influential factors.
In addition to the above issues, the most challenging problem is that
the evacuation strategies can guarantee the safety only when they are
tailored to the particular conditions at the target metro stations. Due to
the great variations of influential factors and objectives, the strategies
for improving and optimizing the evacuation at different metro stations
could be very different. For example, during a fire hazard at an under­
ground metro station, how to release the possible heat and toxic smoke
and provide good lighting are challenging tasks. For a large-scale above-
ground metro station, the familiarity of the emergency exits and the
efficiency of the evacuation guidance may become the key factors
deciding the success of an evacuation event. Besides, the available
renovation options for optimizing the evacuation could be different for
different metro stations. Structural changes, such as building a new
emergency exit, may be easy for some suburban metro stations, but it
could be impossible for the urban central stations, which are closely
surrounded by densely constructed buildings. This indicates that the
adaptive strategies specifically made for different scenarios at the target
metro stations should be required to guarantee the effective safety
management in response to any emergency.
The proposed approach in this research aims to address these issues
in the evacuation at metro station scenarios. Then, the research ques­
tions this research puts efforts to explore are: (1) How to construct the
relationship between the influential factors and objectives of the evac­
uation events, with the consideration of the complexity and potential
conflicting between them; (2) How to obtain the adaptive optimization
solutions for the evacuation at metro stations according to different
scenarios. To solve these problems, a hybrid approach with the incor­
poration of the simulation tool, Light Gradient Boosting Machine
(LightGBM), and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm (NSGA-III) is
proposed in this research. The contribution of this research lies in the
developed approach that is able to (i) construct the relationship between
influential factors and objectives based on the simulations of dynamic
features of the evacuation at metro stations and (ii) effectively perform
the evacuation evaluation and provide adaptive strategies for the
evacuation renovation. The tailored adaptive strategies provided from
the proposed approach can be expected to address the failed aspect of
the evacuation event at the target metro station. The developed
approach can be used as a decision tool that enriches the MOO research
on the evacuation problem and enables the investigation of adaptive
strategies according to the specific condition at different metro stations.
The rest of this research is presented as follows. In Section 2, related
topics on the emergency evacuation, MOO, and adaptive optimization
are reviewed. Section 3 explains the procedures of the proposed
approach. A metro station case study is performed in Section 4. Dis­
cussions are further made in Section 5. In Section 6, conclusions and
future works are presented.
2. Literature review
Due to the crucial importance, studies on the evacuation at metro
stations have been conducted by researchers. By studying the evacuation
process under 18 scenarios, Salarian, Mashhadizadeh [8] proposed a
safe zone approach with the attempt of reducing the evacuation time at
metro stations. Hong, Gao [9] developed a pedestrian-simulation soft­
ware to simulate the information spread and passenger evacuation
process at the metro stations. Hu [10] incorporated virtual reality (VR)
into the simulations of the passenger evacuation at metro stations,
which aimed to provide suggestions for improving the layout design of
metro stations. Similarly, Lin et al. [11] developed a VR-based approach
to study the influence of the spatial knowledge of passengers on the
evacuation events, and it was found that the completeness of the spatial
knowledge of passengers exerted a significant impact on the evacuation
efficiency at metro stations. Based on video analysis, Liu and Chen [12]
investigated the motion features of passengers at the metro stations,
especially during the rush hours when the passenger density is extremely
high.
However, very few studies incorporated MOO into the evacuation
evaluation and optimization under the metro station scenarios, even
with the conflicting nature in it (evacuating more passengers in a short
time) [13, 14]. Features of the metro stations make the complex evac­
uation problems even more complicated. Among the challenging tasks
hindering the application of MOO in the evacuation studies at metro
stations, two of them stand out. One is the elusive relationship between
the influential factors and objectives at the metro station scenarios.
Reviewing the evacuation studies under other scenarios, it can be seen
that explicit formulas are often missed between the influential factors
and objectives. Though many influential factors and objectives are
clearly identified in the evacuation problems of metro stations, their
relationships are very elusive and are even changing according to the
variations of different metro stations. Another problem is that a “fit-­
for-all” optimal solution can hardly satisfy the needs for the evacuation
optimization at metro stations. Even all under the metro station sce­
narios, the evacuation events could present disparate features due to the
structure and passenger difference. That is, it is crucial that the opti­
mized solutions could be specially tailored to solve the problems under
different conditions.
Incorporating adaptive optimization, then, becomes necessary for
the safety management at metro stations, for fulfilling the requirement
of different optimal solutions for different scenarios. Adaptive optimi­
zation in engineering fields refers to the optimization method that could
use the data collected during its optimization process to update and
improve the optimization performance [15]. In contrast to the tradi­
tional optimization where the optimization does not take advantage of
the new information gained during its optimization process, the adap­
tive optimization recognizes the conditions could vary over time and
accordingly develops contingency strategies and defines the circum­
stance under which each of the strategies could be implemented [16].
Considering the high complexity feature at metro stations as introduced
above, adaptive optimization becomes essential to address the specific
problems under the different metro station environments. However,
how to realize the adaptive optimization is often neglected in most of the
previous MOO studies, including the MOO in the evacuation research,
even though adaptive optimization is necessary for many problems and

has attracted great attention from researchers.
To address these above gaps, this research attempts to propose an
adaptive multi-objective optimization approach. This proposed
approach is expected to not only be able to model the dynamic features
of passenger evacuation and simultaneously consider the structure fea­
tures at metro stations, but also be able to construct the relationship
between the influential factors and desired objective, which is critical to
realize the effective evacuation evaluation and optimization. In addi­
tion, adaptive strategies for improving evacuation efficiency can be
expected, which greatly enriches the MOO research of evacuation at
metro stations and fills the gap of incorporating the adaptive strategies
for different conditions of different metro stations.
3. Methodology
To incorporate MOO into the evacuation management and realize
adaptive optimization for metro stations, a hybrid approach integrating
simulation, LightGBM, and NSGA-III is proposed in this research. Fig. 1
presents the workflow of the proposed approach. Firstly, a detailed
analysis of the metro station evacuation is conducted, and an evaluation
system is constructed based on the identification of key objectives and
the influential factors. Secondly, a 3D model of the metro station is
constructed for the evacuation simulation. Based on simulations, a
LightGBM-based meta-model is built for evacuation prediction. Thirdly,
by integrating the LightGBM and NSGA-III, the algorithm can auto­
matically realize the evacuation evaluation and provide the adaptive
strategies to address specific evacuation problems.
3.1. Evacuation analysis
A proper evacuation analysis is the prerequisite to achieve the reli­
able evaluation and effective optimization of the evacuation for a spe­
cific metro station. Influential factors and the desired objectives could be
disparate under different scenarios. Through exhaustive review and the
investigation of the target metro station, two evaluation objectives, the
evacuation time and the passenger flow density, are determined as the
criteria for the evacuation event evaluation at the metro station. Besides,
to evaluate the effectiveness and realize the renovation optimization,
another critical factor, cost, is set as an extra objective. That is to say, for
the renovation evaluation and optimization, there are three objectives in
total, i.e., the evacuation time, flow density, and renovation cost. In
addition, the evacuee feature, the station feature, and the evacuation
guidance are identified as three critical influential features contributing
to the evaluation and optimization of the evacuation events at metro
stations. Three sub-influential factors for each of them are identified,
and that is, nine sub-influential factors in total are determined as the
influential factors in the evaluation index system. Fig. 2 presents the
constructed evaluation index system for the evacuation evaluation and
optimization, and Table 1 presents the description of the influential
factors. Detailed discussions are presented as follows.
(1) Evacuation objectives
As introduced above, the evacuation events under different scenarios
could be very different. Due to the features of the metro stations, the
objectives (i.e., the evacuation time, the evacuation density, and the
cost) are determined as the objectives for the evaluation and renovation
optimization of the evacuation. Among these three objectives, the
evacuation time and density are directly related to the evacuation
evaluation at metro stations. The evacuation time is critical to the suc­
cess of the evacuation at metro stations. Given a metro station, the path
in metro stations is often long and narrow, the density of passenger flow
could be extremely high, especially in the peak hours, and a very limited
time can be allowed for the evacuation in such an environment. Mean­
while, the density is regarded as an indispensable objective for assessing
the success of the evacuation. A too high density in the evacuation could
further produce higher pressures on the evacuees, which could raise the
panic levels and finally lead to high evacuation risks.
For the evacuation renovation optimization, besides the two above
objectives, the objective of the cost in renovation should be considered.
Cost is one of the most important factors that are directly related to the
feasibility of any renovation plans [22]. Especially, metro stations are
often constructed in the central parts of cities, where a huge expenditure
might be needed for the renovation. Hence, the cost issue is included as
one of the objectives considered in evacuation optimization.
(1) Key influential factors
Based on the features of metro stations, influential factors from three
aspects are determined, i.e., the evacuee feature, the station feature, and
the evacuation guidance. The evacuee feature is referring to the key
features of the high-volume passengers commuting at the metro stations.
The station feature refers to the critical station parts that are closely
related to the evacuation events. The evacuation guidance involves the
promptness and effectiveness of the guidance in the evacuation event at
metro stations. For each aspect, three sub-factors are determined.
Detailed analyses of these three aspects and their respective sub-factors
are presented as follows.
Regarding the evacuee feature at metro stations, one of the most
striking features is the highly dense number of passengers (passenger
volume x1) [9]. It is directly related to the evacuation time and density,
and naturally, it becomes one of the most critical factors influencing the
evacuation. The average walking speed (x2) of the passengers is set as
another influential factor of the evacuee features in metro stations.
Despite a great diversity of people in the passenger groups, (female and
male, children and elderly), stability and balance of the crowds could be
reached, especially during the peak hours. The composition of different
people is relatively stable, and the walking speed of individuals may
have to be largely dependent on the speed of the crowds [23]. Another
important feature of the passengers is the herding behavior rate (x3)
during the evacuation events. Under the emergency and pressure, a
passenger could show a tendency to blindly follow the crowd flow

without a clear judgment. Especially under the metro station scenarios
where the space is often narrow and the vision could be very limited, the
panic could be produced during the evacuation and it raises the herding
behavior rate [24]. The herding behavior could push the crowds to
eventually move to the same jammed exits, which could significantly
hamper the evacuation events. Therefore, the proportion of herding
behavior is set as one influential factor for the evacuation evaluation and
optimization.
For the station structure, many factors related to the station condi­
tion should be considered. Due to the fact that the target station is
constructed in the center of the city, where land is an extremely valuable
resource, construction extension is nearly impossible. The renovation of
the station for the safe evacuation mainly focuses on the rationality of its
own structure. Three sub-factors, the number of fare gates (x4), the
number of exits (x5), and obstacles (x6) are considered as sub-factors of
the station structure in this research. Fare gates are used as the necessary
passages for passengers to leave the station, and the number of fare gates
may exert a direct influence on the efficiency of the evacuation [25].
Exits obviously play critical roles in the evacuation event, since more
exits have a great potential of reducing the evacuation time [26]. The
existence of obstacles is considered in this research, because the in­
teractions between passengers and the obstacles often play critical roles
in evacuation events [27]. It is common that different kinds of obstacles
in the metro station, such as the cleaning machines, service desks,
advertising boards, are observed in the stations.
For the evacuation guidance, three sub-factors, i.e., the effectiveness
of signages (x7), the position of the ushers (x8), and the number of ushers
(x9), are added into the evaluation system. Effective signages could help
passengers find the paths and emergency exits in a short time and
disperse the crowds to less dense exits. The rationality and effectiveness
of the signages are decisive to the success of evacuation events [28].
However, effective signages may not be enough for the emergency
evacuation. During the evacuation process, the rate of panic among
passengers could be evidently raised, and unexpected behaviors could
happen, such as the pedestrian counterflow, which could be a disaster
for the evacuation . Thus, proper evacuation guidance by emergency
ushers is especially important. Due to the limited number of available
ushers, the positions of the ushers, i.e., where the ushers are supposed to
stand to guide, is a factor playing a critical role in the evacuation events,
and it should not be ignored [29].
3.2. Evacuation simulation and meta-model construct
Studies have proved that simulations could qualitatively and quan­
titatively reproduce the evacuation process of pedestrians, and the
strategies and lessons from simulations could be very helpful and pro­
vide suggestions to improve the evacuation in the real situation . This
research adopted Anylogic to conduct the evacuation simulations under
different scenarios at the target metro station. To obtain sufficient data
of the evacuation events at the target metro station, orthogonal exper­
imental design (OED) experiments (using the constructed model to
simulate the evacuations under different scenarios) are conducted.
Then, one of the most efficient decision tree based algorithms,
LightGBM, is incorporated into this research to build the meta-model.
After constructing the LightGBM-based meta-model, a sensitivity anal­

3.3. Adaptive optimization
Adaptive optimization recognizes that the evacuation conditions
could be changing over time and different station environments. Rather
than a pre-determined renovation plan based on the current knowledge,
adaptive optimization provides solutions (strategies) according to the
timely obtained information, and solutions could target the problems
under specific scenarios. Fig. 3 illustrates the process of realizing the
automatic evaluation of the evacuation for the station and the adaptive
optimization. This dynamic process mainly consists of three steps, i.e.,
the scenario determination, LightGBM and NSGA-III based optimization,
and adaptive strategy decision. In the first step, the observed scenario
parameters, i.e., the passenger volume, walking speed, and the herding
behavior rate, are put into the algorithm for the primary scenario
evaluation. Step 2 is to apply the NSGA-III optimization, and Step 3 is to
make adaptive strategy decisions that could optimize the evacuation for
the particular scenario. Detailed descriptions are presented as follows.
(1) Evaluation and scenario determination
Collecting the data of the passengers (evacuee features) at the target
station and putting them into the algorithm, the evacuation condition of
the target metro station can be automatically evaluated with the con­
structed meta-model in the algorithm. As analyzed above, two critical
objectives, the evacuation time and density, are determined as the fac­
tors for the evaluation of the evacuation at metro stations. Then, the
failing evacuation scenarios can be identified. Scenarios could be
decided according to these two criteria, where the evacuation standard
(St) is set as 360 s based on the code for safety evacuation [30] and the
density standard (Sd) is set as 3.6 unit/m2 according to the study of Pan,
Qi [31]. In other words, the upper bound value of them represents a safe
evacuation at metro stations. The evacuation events at metro stations
can be evaluated according to these two standards.
Accordingly, four scenarios in total could be identified based on the
two criteria. The first one is that both the evacuation time and the
density are within the standards, which means that the evacuation can
be regarded as a safe evacuation, and this scenario does not require
optimization. Thus, the possible evacuation events that need to be
optimized could be determined as three different scenarios. Scenario I
includes cases where the evacuation density fails but the evacuation
time is within the standard. Scenario II refers to the cases where the
evacuation time fails but the evacuation density is within the standard.
Scenario III is referring to those cases where both the evacuation time
and density fail according to the requirement.
With the evaluated results (identifying the failed cases), optimization
rules are analyzed according to different scenarios. As analyzed, three
objectives in total are determined for the renovation optimization of the
evacuation at metro stations, and all three objectives are the less the
better. Besides, there are two standards required for the evacuation time
and density that should be considered in the optimization rule. Ac­
cording to the three typical scenarios as analyzed above, the corre­
sponding optimization rules can be expressed as follows.

Because two standards exist, the basic optimization rule is to make
both of them within the standards if possible. Thus, in Scenario I, the
evacuation time is within the standard, then the evacuation time is
transformed to a constraint, which can guarantee that it won’t fail even
if the evacuation time would be degraded to some extent to improve the
density at the possibly least cost. In the same way, the density is trans­
formed to a constraint in Scenario II. Scenario III has two sub-steps for
the optimization. Firstly, by setting the evaluated density as a constraint
(guarantee that the density won’t be degraded anymore), optimizations
with the objectives of the evacuation time and cost are conducted. Then,
an evaluation is conducted to check if the evacuation time can be
optimized within the standard. If can, the evacuation time is trans­
formed to be a constraint, the objectives become the minimum of the
density and cost. If cannot, the optimizations, with the objectives of the
time and cost and with the constraint on the density, will continue until
the convergency.
(1) NSGA-III based adaptive optimization
NSGA has been one of the most widely used MOO algorithms in the
past years. NSGA-III has been regarded as a better choice when dealing
with more complicated MOO problems [32], where the mechanism of
well-spread reference points is integrated to maintain the solution di­
versity. Considering the complexity between the objectives of the opti­
mization for the evacuation and the attempt to gain diverse optimization
results, NSGA-III is adopted in this research. The pseudo coding for the
automatic evaluation and seeking the optimal evacuation solutions
using LightGBM and NSGA-III is presented in Algorithm 1. After the
automatic evaluation of the evacuation cases, i.e., gaining scenarios that
at least one of the objectives fails, an NSGA-III based algorithm begins to
search for the adaptive optimization results for the identified cases. To
start the NSGA-III process, an initial population can be produced based
on the scenario parameters, and the population is ranked according to
the evaluation criteria. Three operations, including selection, crossover,
and mutation, are performed to produce the offspring. The next gener­
ation combing the parent and children population will be ranked again
according to the criteria. This process is repeated until the convergency
(the solution cannot be optimized anymore) or a certain standard is met.
Then, the Pareto front is produced based on the ranked population, and
the decision is made based on the optimization rule.
(1) Decision making
Instead of a single optimal solution, a set of optimal trade-off solu­
tions, a Pareto front, for the conflicting objectives is provided for
improved decision making in the MOO problems [33]. A distance-based
decision rule is incorporated for the decision making. Since no priority is
required between objectives in this research, and all three objectives
comply with the rule of the less the better, the point (0, 0, 0) is regarded
as the ideal point in this research. The solution on the Pareto front with
the shortest distance from the ideal point is determined as the optimal
solution. Objectives, including the evacuation time, density, and cost,
have their own features and are measured in different units. The
determination of the optimal solution should be performed as the
normalization. The normalization for all the three objectives can be
realized using Eq. (6), the distance can be calculated from Eq. (7), and
the original values of all the objectives for the optimized results can be
gained by using Eq. (8).

4. Case study
4.1. Background
Jurong East (JE) massive rapid transit (MRT) station is an elevated
interchange station connecting the North-East line and East-West line in
Jurong East, Singapore. It is located at the heart of Jurong Lake District,
with the surroundings of many shopping malls, bus interchanges, and
hospitals. The station has two levels, where Level 1 is the concourse level
and Level 2 has three platforms for the interchange of four train lines.
Fig. 4 presents the photos from the target MRT station. Through the field
investigation, some important features can be perceived. The station is
often fully packed, as presented in Fig. 4 (b). Along with the rapidly
increasing population, the great number of passengers, especially during
peak hours, has made the station more crowded than it can seemingly
cope with [34]. During peak hours, the station has more than 20 thou­
sand ridership per hour, and sometimes, it could cost ten minutes for
passengers to wait on the platform, passengers are often queueing at the
edge of the other platform [35]. Built in the central of the city, the
station has a very narrow space, and the escalators and stairs have very
limited width (1 m and 1.5 m, respectively), as shown in Fig. 4 (e).
Service and advertising boards, maintenance fences, and tools are
observed at the scene, which all could become an obstacle in the evac­
uation events, as shown in Fig. 4 (c) and (d). Another problem is that
there are barely any signages for the emergency exits, which could
degrade the evacuation efficiency to some extent.
4.2. Evacuation simulation and meta-model construct
In order to simulate the evacuation event in the JE MRT station, a 3D
simulation model is constructed in Anylogic, and based on the simula­
tion model, OED experiments are conducted to construct the meta-
model (the constructed 3D model and the detailed OED parameters
are presented in Section B of supplementary material). To test the reli­
ability of the constructed meta-model, a validation is performed and the
results are presented in Table 5 and Fig. 5. Besides, a SHAP sensitivity is
performed to gain the contribution of different factors to the evacuation
objectives. The sensitivity analysis results are presented in Fig. 6.
(1) The LightGBM-based meta-model presents well-fitted lines for
both the evacuation time and density, as shown in Fig. 5. For the
training data, the values of MAE and RMSE for the evacuation
time are 21.8 and 28.3, respectively, and the indicator of R2 for
the evacuation time is 0.94, as shown in Table 5. The values of
MAE and RMSE for the evacuation density are 0.53 and 0.46,
respectively, and the indicator of R2 for the evacuation time is
0.95. For the test data, the values of MAE and RMSE for the
evacuation time are 31.1 and 32.7, respectively, and the indicator
of R2 for the evacuation time is 0.91. The values of MAE and
RMSE for the evacuation density are 0.77 and 0.49, respectively,
and the indicator of R2 for the evacuation time is 0.91. The values
of the error indicators for both the evacuation time and density
are very low, and the robust indicator for both of them demon­
strates high values. The results indicate that the constructed
meta-model demonstrates a high accuracy in the evacuation
result prediction, and it can provide reliable and accurate evac­
uation evaluation results.
(2) The usher position, internal and external exits are identified as
the most important factors, except for the passenger volume. Due
to the nature of the evacuation event at metro stations, it is un­
derstandable that the passenger volume is the most significant
factor contributing to the evacuation time and density. Other
than this, as presented in Fig. 6, for the evacuation time, the usher
positions and the external exits rank the second and third places,
respectively. The number of external exits is directly related to
the completeness of the passenger evacuation. Thus, it is
evidently critical to the evacuation time. For the density, the
usher positions and the internal exits take the second and third
important places, respectively, as presented in Fig. 6. This dem­
onstrates that more internal exits could disperse the crowd and
reduce the density. The usher position ranks the second place for
both the evacuation time and density, indicating the importance
of guidance in the evacuation. That is to say, a proper guidance
could significantly improve the evacuation [29].
(3) The signage and the number of ushers are identified as factors
contributing the least to the evacuation for the evacuation time

4.3. Evaluation and adaptive optimization
A total of 50 cases, representing the evacuation conditions at the
target metro station, are put into the algorithm for evaluation and
optimization. The data of the evacuee features (x1 to x3) are collected
from station sites, and the input factors x4 to x9 are {1, 1, 7, 1, 1, 1,
1} (from Table S2 of supplementary material), which is in accordance
with the real structure condition of the station. Assumptions are made to
perform the simulation-based optimizations: (1) Before the evacuation
starts, passengers are randomly scattered in the station; (2) Movement
speed in the stairwell is around 0.6 m/s when the density is 3.5 unit/m2
or above; (3) Extreme conditions, such as severe stampedes and the
caused consequence, are not considered in this research for simplicity
and operational feasibility; (4) Reaction delay is not considered in the
railway station evacuation scenarios. Passengers would immediately
start finding their ways out when the evacuation alarm starts; (5) Es­
calators stop working but can be used as stairs for passengers to
evacuate.
Gaining the evaluated results, it is found that 17 cases are qualified
(both of the evacuation time and density are within the standards), and
33 evacuation events fail (at least one of the objectives fails). Among
these failing evacuations, 4 cases that fail the time standard (Scenario I),
12 cases that fail the density standards (Scenario II), and 17 cases that
fail both of the time and density (Scenario III) are picked out to perform
the adaptive optimization. The results are presented in Fig. 7. To gain an
idea of how the cases are optimized with the adaptive optimization,
three typical cases (#1, #5, #17 under scenarios I, II, III, respectively)
are selected. Table 6 presents the parameters for conducting the NSGA-
III based adaptive optimization algorithm. Fig. 9 presents the adaptive
optimization process for the failing evacuation case #1. Repeating the
process, all the cases under three scenarios can be adaptively optimized.
The optimized results for three cases and scenarios are presented in
Tables 7 and 8, and a comparison between the original points and the
adaptively optimized results is presented in Fig. 10. Detailed discussions
are presented as follows.
(1) The target station is capable of safely evacuating the passengers
when the passenger volume is no more than 1000. By investi­
gating the simulation results, as presented in Fig. 7, it can be seen
that the evacuation time for the scenarios with 1600 passenger
volumes or less is within the standard. But for the density
objective, cases under the scenarios with 1600 passenger volume
would fail the standard, and failed cases also appear under the
scenarios with 1000 passenger volume. To further investigate the
evacuation ability of the target station, a fitting model is built,
and the results are presented in Fig. 8. As the results demonstrate,
the station could be successfully completed considering the
evacuation time standard when the passenger volume is no more
than 2080, but regarding the density level, the evacuation can
only be safely executed under around 1100 or less passenger
volume scenarios. Combining these two evaluation objectives
together and the results from the simulation results (Fig. 7) and
fitting model (Fig. 8), it can be safely concluded that the target
station could successfully complete the evacuation when the
passenger volume is no more than 1000. This provides a reference
for the metro stations managers that evacuation measures should

5. Discussions
To understand the effectiveness of the adaptive optimization, the
comparison of the adaptive optimization and non-adaptive optimization
is performed in this section. The non-adaptive optimization refers to the
optimization method that taking the evacuation optimization as a
normal MOO problem without any priority and does not differentiate
any specific condition. To be concrete, the reasoning of the non-adaptive
optimization is quite straightforward, looking for the optimal trade-off
solutions of minimizing all three objectives, and whereas, the motiva­
tion of the adaptive optimization is to develop tailored strategies ac­
cording to different conditions. For example, if a case is evaluated as 330
s for the evacuation time and 4.2 unit/m2 for the density. The non-
adaptive optimization would not consider that the evacuation time is
already within the standard but directly seek the optimal trade-off so­
lutions minimizing the evacuation time and density with potentially
minimized cost. In adaptive optimization, the condition that the evac­
uation time already meets the standard is recognized, and the algorithm
is attempting to find the trade-off solutions to minimize the density with
a minimized cost on the premise that the evacuation time would not fail.
In other words, the non-adaptive optimization applies the only rule,
minimizing the objectives, to find the optimal trade-off solutions for all
failing cases, while the adaptive optimization evaluates the features of
how the cases are failing and then looking for tailored optimal trade-off
solutions particularly for each of the cases. The non-adaptive optimi­
zation rule is presented as in the following Eqs. (16) and (17). The de­
cision rule to obtain the optimal solution is the same as the one for
conducting the adaptive optimization proposed in Section 3.3 Eqs. (10)
to (12).

follows.
(1) The adaptive optimization demonstrates a higher cost efficiency,
compared to the non-adaptive optimization. As presented in
Table 9 and Fig. 13, the cost efficiency for the three typical cases
under adaptive optimization are 1.16, 0.56, and 1.15, respec­
tively. These are higher than the cost efficiency under the non-
adaptive optimization, which are 0.45, 0.33, and 0.61, respec­
tively. Besides, as presented in Fig. 14, the optimal solutions from
adaptive optimization are better (closer to the ideal point) than
solutions from non-adaptive optimization. It indicates that the
adaptive optimization is not only capable of successfully
completing the optimization tasks (the objectives of the evacua­
tion time and density of all three typical cases are within the
standards after optimization), but also be more efficient by
identifying the different features of different cases and seeking
solutions to address those specific problems in the failing cases.
The results in Table 10 confirm this point. As presented, an
overall average cost efficiency, 2.04, can be achieved for the
adaptive optimization, which is a lot higher than the average
efficiency of the non-adaptive optimization, 0.57. In addition, the
average cost efficiency values of all the 33 failing cases for Sce­
narios I, II, and III under the adaptive optimization are 1.74, 3.41
and 1.14, which are all higher than the values under the non-
adaptive optimization, which are 0.93, 0.43 and 0.60, respec­
tively. These results fully embody the benefit of adopting adap­
tive optimization, i.e., providing solutions good enough but
won’t consume too much to solve the problem.
(2) The adaptive optimization presents a strong reliability. To further
test the reliability of the proposed approach, simulations of the 33
cases in the Anylogic model are conducted. After gaining the
optimal solutions for the 33 cases, the solution settings are put
back into the simulation models constructed in Anylogic, and the
evaluated results are gained by running the simulations for the 33
cases. A validation test is performed by comparing the adaptively
optimized results gained from the optimization algorithm with
the results gained from the simulations of Anylogic models, and
the results are presented in Fig. 15. As shown in the figure, well-
fitted lines and relatively high R2 results are gained for both the
evacuation time and density (0.9246 and 0.9787, respectively).
From this validation test, it can be concluded that a strong reli­
ability of the proposed approach is demonstrated.

conflicting between the evacuation objectives, few studies focused on
solving the multi-objective optimization problem of the evacuation
events under metro station scenarios. Especially, even though tailored
evacuation strategies are required to realize the effective evacuation
management, very few studies investigated the methods of looking for
adaptive strategies for the renovation optimization of evacuation at
metro stations. This research proposes an approach integrating the
simulation method, LightGBM, and NSGA-III to explore the methods for
the automatic evacuation evaluation and adaptive optimization. A
simulation tool is used to simulate the dynamic process of the passenger
evacuation at metro stations. LightGBM is used to construct meta-
models to reveal the relationship between influential factors and ob­
jectives of the evacuation events. A hybrid of LightGBM and NSGA-III is
used to perform the adaptive optimization under varying conditions. A
real metro station is studied with the proposed approach to test its
effectiveness.
Through the case study, it is found that: (1) A total 33 of the tested 50
cases are identified as the failing cases, at least of the objectives fails the
objective standard, and it is revealed that for the studied target metro
station, the evacuation could be executed successfully when the pas­
senger volume is no more than 1000, but very likely to fail when a
higher volume exists; (2) For all the three identified scenarios, the
proposed approach could provide the adaptive optimization strategies
according to the corresponding conditions, and an average 24.8% of the
improvement degree can be realized; (3) Comparatively, the adaptive
multi-objective optimization demonstrates a better average cost effi­
ciency, 2.04, which is significantly higher than the average cost effi­
ciency of the non-adaptive optimization, 0.57. Through the case study, it
is demonstrated that even with the complexity and conflict between the
influential factors and objectives, the proposed approach provides an
innovative method, constructing the meta-model, to effectively find the
relationship between them and realize the evacuation evaluation.
Furthermore, the consideration of MOO and adaptive optimization so­
lutions in this research can be expected to greatly enrich the MOO in­
vestigations of the evacuation events, and also provide the tailored
strategies according to different scenarios, which are necessary for
realizing more efficient and cost-effective measures of the evacuation
optimization at metro stations.
Improvement can be expected for the proposed approach. A more
comprehensive control and management of the metro station can be
expected by upgrading the proposed approach, i.e., to construct a digital
twin aided evacuation audit for the metro stations. More sensor-based
data could be included in the adaptive evaluation and optimization
model. For example, with the integration of the camera, not only the
passenger volume can be gained, the counterflow during the evacuation
process can be timely perceived. As the counterflows could seriously
hamper the evacuation process, the incorporation of more real-time data
could be used to inform project managers to allocate the resource
(evacuation ushers in this case) more effectively according to new up­
dates and feedback. Uncertainties underlying data monitoring and
measurement (e.g., human behaviors) will be further considered in
MOO [37], and the corresponding adaptive strategies can then better
guarantee the success of the evacuation events.
